concepts.label: SQL++ for Analytics Data Types (primitive / special / composite)
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - the page-level type scheme. Named to parallel the sibling extraction-layer concept n1ql:data-types (cloud/n1ql/n1ql-language-reference/datatypes.json), but kept as a separate id: this page's own three-way primitive/special/composite classification and its MULTISET member have no counterpart in the n1ql:data-types record, which lists MISSING, NULL, Boolean, Numbers, String, Array, Object and Binary with no such grouping and no multiset.

concepts.label: Primitive type (SQL++ for Analytics)
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - one of the page's own three named type categories (BOOLEAN, STRING, BIGINT, DOUBLE).

concepts.label: Special type (SQL++ for Analytics)
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - one of the page's own three named type categories (NULL, MISSING).

concepts.label: Composite type (SQL++ for Analytics)
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - one of the page's own three named type categories (OBJECT, ARRAY, MULTISET).

concepts.label: Multiset (SQL++ for Analytics data type)
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - an unordered collection type permitting duplicate elements, distinct from Array (ordered, from incoming JSON). No sibling concept exists anywhere in the corpus (checked: no promoted or extraction-layer 'multiset' id in concepts/ or extractions/) - this is a genuinely Analytics-specific SQL++ data type with no counterpart documented for SQL++ for Query, which n1ql:data-types lists as having only MISSING, NULL, Boolean, Numbers, String, Array, Object and Binary.

concepts.label: Temporal data representation (SQL++ for Analytics)
concepts.reused_or_minted: minted - the pattern by which SQL++ for Analytics represents dates/times/timestamps: not as a dedicated data type, but as ordinary `string` or `bigint` values interpreted by temporal functions.

relations.subject: analytics:primitive-type
relations.evidence: An instance of Couchbase Analytics data model can be a **_primitive type_** (`BOOLEAN`, `STRING`, `BIGINT`, or `DOUBLE`), a **_special type_** (`NULL` or `MISSING`), or a **_composite type_** (`OBJECT`, `ARRAY`, or `MULTISET`).

relations.evidence: An instance of Couchbase Analytics data model can be a **_primitive type_** (`BOOLEAN`, `STRING`, `BIGINT`, or `DOUBLE`), a **_special type_** (`NULL` or `MISSING`), or a **_composite type_** (`OBJECT`, `ARRAY`, or `MULTISET`).

relations.subject: analytics:multiset-type
relations.evidence: A `multiset` cannot appear in the incoming JSON. A `multiset` is converted into a JSON array with an undefined order of elements in the query results.

relations.subject: analytics:data-types
relations.evidence: Since JSON does not provide data types for temporal data, SQL++ for Analytics uses the `string` and `bigint` types for this purpose. SQL++ for Analytics provides many builtin functions, called temporal functions, that operate on `string` or `bigint` values, interpreting them as dates or times.

notable_absence.finding: This page names no Binary type at all, where the sibling n1ql:data-types record (cloud/n1ql/n1ql-language-reference/datatypes.json) documents one explicitly ('the value is exposed as binary'). Whether SQL++ for Analytics has no binary-value handling, or simply doesn't document it on this page, cannot be determined from this page alone.

cross_component_finding: This page's own three-way classification - primitive (BOOLEAN, STRING, BIGINT, DOUBLE), special (NULL, MISSING), composite (OBJECT, ARRAY, MULTISET) - has no counterpart grouping in the sibling n1ql:data-types record, which lists MISSING, NULL, Boolean, Numbers, String, Array, Object and Binary as a flat list with no primitive/special/composite split. The sharpest single difference is MULTISET: an unordered, duplicate-permitting composite type that is a first-class member of this page's type system ('A `multiset` is an unordered collection of items. A `multiset` allows multiple instances of its elements.') and appears nowhere in the Query-service type reference. Both dialects, however, converge on the same workaround for temporal data: this page states 'Since JSON does not provide data types for temporal data, SQL++ for Analytics uses the `string` and `bigint` types for this purpose', while the n1ql:data-types record's own evidence states 'SQL++ does not support the Date data type; however SQL++ does provide a full range of functions which you can use to manipulate dates' - independently-worded statements of the identical design choice (no dedicated date type; string/numeric-plus-functions instead), which is a genuine point of dialect convergence rather than divergence, though the numeric type used differs (BIGINT epoch-millis vs presumably NUMBER on the Query side) and is left uncompared since the Query-side numeric type isn't stated per-function on that record.
